display.story_text:
Thursday night, Soldier Field, a short week for both teams, and the number says Chicago by 3. I say the number is a field goal too generous to the home team.

Here's the setup: New England Patriots (4-2) at Chicago Bears (4-2), 8:15 p.m. ET on Prime Video. The consensus has Chicago −3 with a total of 50.5 (Oct 20, 12:52 UTC). My card: New England Patriots +3, Under 50.5, and a final of Patriots 24, Bears 21.

Why the Patriots? Because the season-long numbers don't see two equal teams. The Formula rates New England at 1.6 and Chicago at −4.5. Give the Bears 1.75 points for Soldier Field and the Patriots still come out 4.4 points better. That's a road team that should be laying a little, getting 3 instead. Drake Maye has thrown at least three touchdown passes in three straight games, and the Patriots have won three in a row.

Now, the honest caveat, because I don't sell sunshine: New England finished Sunday's win over the Jets without right tackle Morgan Moses, left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and right guard Ben Brown, and the official Week 7 injury report isn't out yet. Chicago's pass rush gets home on 9.7% of dropbacks, and Kyler Gordon just posted three sacks and two forced fumbles in Atlanta. If that line is held together with tape on Thursday, Maye will feel it. That's the status to watch all week.

Why the Under? Because these defenses don't hand out points. New England has allowed 113 in six games, and Chicago 119. The Formula's number is 43.2, and my final is 45, more than five points shy of the posted 50.5. Caleb Williams is back from a hamstring and was sharp last week, but the Bears also handed out a pile of penalty yards in Atlanta, and drives that stall on flags don't end in touchdowns.

Now, the room didn't agree, and you know I love it when the room doesn't agree.

Follow The Money makes no pick, but its market split is Bears 27, Patriots 24. The Formula's score is Patriots 24, Bears 19. Opposite winners. The Formula fired back: "Bears by three on a short week, with Maye this hot? Bold."

Follow The Money didn't blink: "Home team, Thursday night, and a pass rush that just lived in Atlanta's backfield. Bring earmuffs."

Next Man Up and Letdown Watch both landed on Patriots 24, Bears 19 and stayed out of it. In The Trenches passed on a pick, borrowed The Formula's score and went right back to staring at New England's banged-up offensive line.

Bottom of the card: the Patriots don't need to win this game to cash +3. They just need to keep it inside a field goal, and I think they win it outright.

Patriots 24, Bears 21. Patriots cover the 3. Under 50.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Thursday night at Soldier Field, 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Prime Video. Two 4-2 teams, a short week for both, and two insiders who have been texting each other since Sunday afternoon. Walt Brenner keeps the Bears' family tree. Glen Tolliver keeps the Patriots' receipts. Gloves off, manners on.

Walt: Welcome to Soldier Field, Glen. Columns out front, the lake out back, and a city all around it. We play football in a city. You play next to a lighthouse in the suburbs.

Glen: The lighthouse is a nice touch, Walt. So are the six Super Bowl banners. How many do you have again?

Walt: One Super Bowl, plus eight NFL championships from before the Super Bowl existed. We didn't join this league. We built it.

Glen: And you've been telling everyone about it ever since.

Last week, Patriots: New England beat the Jets 26-19 for its third straight win and its fourth straight against New York. Drake Maye threw touchdown passes to Romeo Doubs (a diving 42-yarder), DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry, his third straight game with at least three. The defense, with Christian Gonzalez back from a shoulder injury, held the Jets to 0-for-3 in the red zone.

Glen: Rings are receipts, but process wins the next one, and the process was sloppy. Two lost fumbles. And we lost three offensive linemen during the game: right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and right guard Ben Brown (knee). Doubs left with a shoulder injury too. With no official report out yet, that's the status sheet I'm watching all week.

Last week, Bears: Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury that cost him three games and completed his first 12 passes in Atlanta. Bears 31, Falcons 23.

Walt: And Kyler Gordon, activated off the PUP list before the game, had three sacks and two forced fumbles. From a cornerback! Bronko Nagurski would have stood up and clapped.

Glen: You also had more yellow flags in that game than a parade has streamers.

Walt: We like to keep the officials involved. It's a community thing.

The matchup: This one starts up front. A patched-together New England front five meets a Chicago pass rush that just sacked Michael Penix Jr. five times, three of them by a cornerback. Maye has thrown at least three touchdown passes in each of his last three games, and A.J. Brown is back from injured reserve after three catches against the Jets. On the other side, Ben Johnson's offense has its quarterback back, and Williams shares the ball: Burden, Loveland, Rome Odunze and Swift all got touches last week. Mike Vrabel and coordinator Zak Kuhr will try to keep Williams in the pocket. Chicago's Dennis Allen will try to make Maye see ghosts.

The numbers: Chicago has scored 150 points and allowed 119. New England has scored 136 and allowed 113. These two are as even as a Lake Michigan breeze is stubborn.

Glen: Speaking of which, Walt, does the wind off the lake count as a 12th man, or do you just blame it for the punts?

Walt: The wind is a Bear, Glen. It's been on the roster longer than either of us. Your wind is a cranberry bog breeze.

Glen: Last thing. We were in Super Bowl LX in February. We lost it to Seattle, 29-13, and I'll own that. When was your last February?

Walt: Long enough ago that the Shuffle was on the radio. It still holds up, by the way.

Glen: It does not.

Respect to both: two young quarterbacks, two first-place hopes, one Thursday night beneath the lights by the lake.

My call: Patriots 24, Bears 21.

display.story_text:
The NFL's first regular-season game in France kicks off at breakfast time back home, and I'm taking the team that just learned how to win ugly on the road.

Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) vs. New Orleans Saints (2-4) at the Stade de France, Saint-Denis, Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET on NFL Network. It's a neutral site with the Saints as the designated home team. The consensus has Pittsburgh −3.5 with a total of 44.5 (Oct 20, 12:52 UTC). My card: Pittsburgh Steelers −3.5, Over 44.5, and a final of Steelers 27, Saints 22.

Why Pittsburgh? Because the gap between these teams is bigger than a field goal. The Formula rates New Orleans at −12.2 and Pittsburgh at −5.8. With no home field on a neutral pitch, that's Steelers by 6.5, and you're asked to lay only 3.5. Aaron Rodgers just led four fourth-quarter scoring drives in Tampa to erase a 13-point hole, and DK Metcalf was targeted 15 times. New Orleans has allowed 178 points in six games. That's a lot of rope to give a quarterback who has seen every defense ever drawn up.

Why the Over? Both of these teams have shown you they'll put points on the board. New Orleans' young offense can get hot in a hurry, and Pittsburgh's defense has been in some long afternoons. The Formula's number is 49.6, and my final adds up to 49. That's four and a half points of cushion on a 44.5.

The honest worry: Tyler Shough is playing through broken bones in his non-throwing hand, and the official Week 7 injury report isn't out yet. Pittsburgh was also missing receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson in Tampa. Watch both of those this week.

Now, the room. Everybody has Pittsburgh winning, but not by the same amount, and not with the same points. Follow The Money makes no pick, but its market split is Steelers 24, Saints 21, a three-point game. The Formula has Steelers 28, Saints 22, a six-point game.

The Formula opened fire: "A three-point game? Rodgers just dragged this team out of a hole in Tampa. Give the man some credit, pal."

Follow The Money had a reply ready: "It's a neutral field at breakfast time. Nobody's body clock knows what day it is, including yours."

Neither one blinked. Next Man Up and Letdown Watch both have 28-22 and are keeping their heads down. In The Trenches passed on a pick, borrowed that score and asked everyone to please stop yelling in French.

Bottom of the card: a better team, a short number, and two offenses that have found the end zone lately. Pittsburgh by four or more, and enough points to clear 44.5.

Steelers 27, Saints 22. Steelers cover the 3.5. Over 44.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Bonjour from Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, where the Stade de France hosts the first NFL regular-season game ever played in France. Kickoff is 2:30 in the afternoon in Paris, 9:30 a.m. Eastern on NFL Network, with croissants for breakfast and football for brunch. The Saints are the designated home team. Ed Kowalski speaks for Pittsburgh's six Lombardi Trophies. Andre Thibault speaks for New Orleans, a city with a French accent of its own.

Andre: Let's settle something first, Ed. This is a home game for us in every way that matters. La Nouvelle-Orléans. The French Quarter. We're basically visiting cousins.

Ed: Cute. Pittsburgh has a little history with the French too, Andre. Ask anybody down at the Point about the old forts. I don't bring it up to be rude. I bring it up because we never forget anything.

Andre: That's the most Pittsburgh thing anyone has ever said. You brought a centuries-old grudge to a football game in Paris.

Ed: Continuity, Andre. We don't let things go. Not grudges, not coaches, not the Terrible Towel in my glove box.

Last week, Steelers: Pittsburgh trailed Tampa Bay 16-3 entering the fourth quarter and won 26-19 in overtime. Jamel Dean, a former Buccaneer, set up a field goal with an interception and a 40-yard return, and Jalen Ramsey ended it with a fourth-down sack. Pittsburgh played without receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson because of injuries.

Ed: Chuck Noll would have hated the first three quarters and loved the last one. Rodgers got sacked five times early and kept coming back to Metcalf. That's the whole Steelers lesson in one afternoon: you get knocked down, you get back up and throw it to the big guy.

Last week, Saints: Tyler Shough threw touchdown passes to rookie Bryce Lance (his first NFL catch for a score), Alvin Kamara and Chris Olave, and ran for another. Cornerback Martin Emerson intercepted two passes, and Isaiah Stalbird forced a kickoff fumble just before halftime that flipped the whole game. Shough has been playing through broken bones in his left, non-throwing hand.

Andre: I love this team because we grow our own. Shough, Lance, Stalbird. Kellen Moore calls the plays, and those kids are learning to finish. They also learned that a 24-point cushion in New Jersey can shrink in a hurry. We'll work on it on the flight.

The matchup: Start with T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Cam Heyward against a Saints offensive front protecting a young quarterback with a sore hand. Then flip it: Cam Jordan, Chase Young and Carl Granderson against a 42-year-old Rodgers who got hit plenty in Tampa. Both defenses use a 3-4 base. Metcalf against Kool-Aid McKinstry is the one-on-one to circle. For New Orleans, Kamara is still the Swiss Army knife, and Olave is the deep threat.

The numbers: Pittsburgh has scored 137 and allowed 128. New Orleans has scored 152 and allowed 178.

Andre: One more thing, Ed. Your coach, Mike McCarthy, once beat the Steelers in a Super Bowl when he coached Green Bay.

Ed: And now he works for us. That's how you win a rivalry. You hire it.

Andre: We'll have beignets on the sideline. You'll have pierogies.

Ed: And the Eiffel Tower will have a Terrible Towel on it by halftime.

Bon match to both sides, and a big welcome to every French fan seeing their first live NFL game.

My call: Steelers 27, Saints 22.

display.story_text:
The best team in this game is also the one flying cross-country on a short week. I'm laying the points anyway, and I'll tell you why.

San Francisco 49ers (6-0) at Atlanta Falcons (2-4), Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on Fox at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The consensus has San Francisco −3.5 with a total of 50.5 (Oct 20, 12:52 UTC). My card: San Francisco 49ers −3.5, Under 50.5, and a final of 49ers 27, Falcons 22.

Why the 49ers? The Formula rates San Francisco at 8.1 and Atlanta at 0.4. Even after giving the Falcons 1.75 for home field, that's 49ers by 5.9. You're laying 3.5. Atlanta is 0-3 at home, and its last two games brought an overtime loss to Baltimore, in which Michael Penix Jr. left with a rib injury, and a 31-7 hole against Chicago. San Francisco, meanwhile, protects its quarterback like a vault. The 49ers allow sacks on 2.9% of dropbacks. Atlanta allows them on 8.8%, and Chicago just sacked Penix five times.

The caveats, because I don't hide the ugly parts: the 49ers beat Washington 23-17 on Monday night and now travel to Atlanta on a short week, and a six-point win over a 1-4-1 team at home was not exactly a statement. Also, the Falcons run for 5.2 yards a carry. If Bijan Robinson gets more than nine carries this time, Atlanta can shorten the game.

Why the Under? The Formula's number is 48.5, and my final adds up to 49. That's a point and a half short of 50.5. San Francisco has allowed 110 points in six games. Both teams' run defenses are stingy, 3.7 yards a carry allowed by San Francisco and 3.8 by Atlanta, and the 49ers can grind clock with Christian McCaffrey.

The room agreed on the winner, and that's where the peace ended. The Formula, Next Man Up and Letdown Watch all have 49ers 27, Falcons 21, and In The Trenches passed on a pick and borrowed that score. Follow The Money's market split is 49ers 27, Falcons 24, and it is the only one in the room that likes the Over 50.5, because the total has climbed a full point since it opened.

Of course, The Formula still found one: "Twenty-four for Atlanta? Against this defense? Did you watch a different Falcons team than I did?"

Follow The Money didn't even look up: "This week I'm on the Over and you're on the Under. Same game, opposite sides. We'll see who's still talking on Monday."

Everybody else stayed out of it.

Bottom of the card: a better, cleaner team getting a short number against a club that can't win at home yet. Lay it and take the Under.

49ers 27, Falcons 22. 49ers cover the 3.5. Under 50.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Mercedes-Benz Stadium, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox. San Francisco arrives 6-0 and on a short week after Monday night's 23-17 home win against Washington. Atlanta arrives 2-4 and still looking for its first home win. Nora Haskell measures the 49ers in rings, all five of them. Russ Amundsen measures the Falcons in NFC South math, and the math says nothing is decided in October.

Russ: Nora, welcome to Atlanta. Our roof opens like a camera lens. Look up and be amazed.

Nora: I've heard. I've also heard you're 0-3 at home.

Russ: We're saving the good stuff. The NFC South gets settled in December. Ask anybody.

Nora: Five Super Bowls, Russ. Montana, Young, Walsh. The Catch. Our trophy case has its own zip code.

Russ: And your defensive coordinator used to be our head coach. Raheem Morris coached the Falcons the last two seasons. So technically, our guy is running your defense.

Nora: Technically, we hired him. So technically, he's ours now.

Last game, 49ers: On Monday night, the 49ers beat Washington 23-17 at home to stay perfect. Before that, the 49ers won 32-29 in Seattle in a playoff rematch with the defending champions. Brock Purdy found Mike Evans four times for 75 yards on the go-ahead drive, then hit newcomer Brandin Cooks for a 7-yard touchdown, and Evans caught the 2-point conversion. After Seattle tied it, Purdy drove the 49ers into range for Eddy Pineiro's go-ahead field goal with 1:56 left. The game had seven combined turnovers, a season high.

Nora: I don't get excited about October. I get excited about February. But Evans going up and getting the ball in Seattle? I'll allow myself one smile.

Last week, Falcons: Atlanta fell behind Chicago 31-7 and rallied to 31-23 before a late strip-sack ended it. Michael Penix Jr., a week after leaving the Baltimore game with a rib injury, threw three touchdown passes: a 13-yarder to Jahan Dotson and two to Kyle Pitts. Penix also threw two 2-point conversions, to Zachariah Branch and Drake London. But the Bears sacked him five times, and Bijan Robinson got just nine carries. And the scariest moment of the day ended in the best way: rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels was carted off with a neck injury, then walked back into the locker room on his own after a hospital visit. Praise God for that.

Russ: Kevin Stefanski said the slow start was on the coaches. I agree. Bijan Robinson with nine carries is like owning a sports car and leaving it in the garage.

The matchup: The Falcons run for 5.2 yards a carry, and San Francisco allows just 3.7. That's the heavyweight fight. Christian McCaffrey against Jessie Bates III and the Falcons' second level could decide it, and Atlanta may be short-handed at linebacker after Daniels' injury and Divine Deablo's arm injury. Purdy has been sacked rarely this year. Penix has not. Nick Bosa against the Falcons' tackles is the one-on-one to watch.

The numbers: Atlanta has scored 142 and allowed 153. San Francisco has scored 177 and allowed 110 through six games, all wins.

Nora: One more, Russ. Remind me who won the last time these two franchises met in a Super Bowl?

Russ: We've never met in a Super Bowl, Nora.

Nora: Exactly. One of us keeps getting there.

Russ: That's cold. I'm going to go eat a peach and think about the standings.

Here's a sentence you don't get to write often: I think the Browns win this game, and I'm still taking the Titans.

Cleveland Browns (4-2) at Tennessee Titans (1-5), Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on CBS at Nissan Stadium. The consensus has Cleveland −1.5 with a total of 38.5 (Oct 20, 12:52 UTC). My card: Tennessee Titans +1.5, Under 38.5, and a final of Browns 19, Titans 18.

Why take the points with a team I think loses? Because one point is the whole story here. The Formula rates Tennessee at −9.4 and Cleveland at −7.2. Give the Titans 1.75 for home field and it's Browns by 0.5. That's a coin flip with a road team laying a point and a half. When the honest number is half a point, I want the side that gets the hook.

And look at how Cleveland wins. All four Browns victories came down to the final moments. That's a team living on a tightrope, and tightropes snap both ways. Tennessee just won its first game, 26-20 in Indianapolis, with six sacks, three takeaways and a blocked punt for a touchdown. The Titans' defense is real.

Why the Under? Because these offenses haven't earned 38.5. The Formula's number is 36.8, and my final adds up to 37. That's a point and a half of room. Both teams run for just 3.8 yards a carry. I'll admit the risk: both teams just found late points, Cleveland with 10 in the fourth quarter and Tennessee with 20 after halftime, and one special-teams score can wreck a low total. But I'll take two offenses that need four quarters to get going.

Now the fun part, because the room split down the middle on the side. The Formula, Next Man Up and Letdown Watch all have the same 19-18 score, and Follow The Money makes no pick, with a market split a point higher on each side at 20-19. In The Trenches borrows that 19-18 score but likes Cleveland −1.5, the exact opposite side from everyone else.

The Formula jumped first: "You want to lay points on the road with a team that needed a last-second kick to beat a backup quarterback? Bold."

In The Trenches was ready: "Same score as you, opposite side. One of us is a genius and one of us is a comedian, and I'm not the one telling jokes."

Next Man Up tried to change the subject. Letdown Watch reminded everybody that the Titans just threw a party on Broadway, and parties come with mornings after. Follow The Money just smiled.

Bottom of the card: if Cleveland wins a low-scoring game by one, which is exactly what I expect, the Titans still cash and the Under comes in. That's the beauty of a hook.

Nissan Stadium, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS. One team has won four games in the final moments. The other just won its first game and partied like it was New Year's Eve on Broadway. Frank Haller carries the Browns' old championship scrolls. Pete Varga carries the Titans' patience, along with the Houston Oilers' first two AFL titles.

Frank: Pete, I'll start nice. Congratulations on the win. Truly. It's a big day when you get the first one.

Pete: Thank you, Frank. I'll be nice too. Congratulations on the four AAFC titles and four NFL championships. Remind me of the most recent one?

Frank: Next question.

Pete: That long, huh?

Frank: We're busy, Pete. Cleveland has the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame to run. You've got a lot of guitars in Nashville, I'll admit. Do any of them play rock?

Pete: We're Music City, Frank. Half the songs on your radio were written on Music Row. We'll lend you a few.

Last week, Browns: Linebacker Carson Schwesinger knocked the ball loose from Derrick Henry, Tyson Campbell recovered, and Audric Estime, signed off Minnesota's practice squad that week, bulled in from 2 yards out to tie it. Browns 13, Ravens 10. Szmyt had missed from 48 a few minutes earlier, and his first try at the winner was blocked, but a Baltimore offside wiped it out.

Frank: Todd Monken spent the last three years running Baltimore's offense. He went back and beat his old friends with a field goal and a fumble. That's how Paul Brown would have drawn it up, if Paul Brown enjoyed suspense, which he did not.

Last week, Titans: Tennessee trailed Indianapolis 13-0 at halftime and won 26-20 for Robert Saleh's first victory as Titans coach. The defense forced three turnovers and posted six sacks, two by Jeffery Simmons, who also forced a Jonathan Taylor fumble on the first play of the second half. Chimere Dike's 58-yard punt return set up the tying touchdown, Cam Ward to rookie Carnell Tate from 8 yards. Then James Williams Sr. blocked a punt and Oluwafemi Oladejo returned it 14 yards for the lead. Joey Slye kicked four field goals, including two in the final 2 1/2 minutes.

Pete: Patience, Frank. Ward is in his second season. He went 11 of 22 last week, and that's fine. Development isn't a straight road. Neither is Interstate 40.

The matchup: This is a defensive game with a capital D. Cleveland's front, with Mason Graham, Jared Verse and Schwesinger, faces a Titans offense that has scored 84 points in six games. Tennessee's front, led by Simmons, faces a Browns offense that has scored 106 and allows sacks at a high clip. Tennessee runs for 3.8 yards a carry. So does Cleveland. Whoever wins the first-down battle probably wins the game.

Watch list: Cleveland running back Quinshon Judkins missed last week with an ankle injury, so his status is one to follow. Tate caught six passes for 70 yards and his first NFL touchdown last week. And the kickers might decide it again: Szmyt and Slye both just won games with their legs.

Frank: Prediction, Pete: you'll get a nice crowd, a nice anthem, and a nice field goal at the end. Ours.

Pete: You've won four games by the skin of your teeth, Frank. That's not a dynasty. That's a cardiologist's dream.

Frank: We call it character.

Pete: We call it Sunday. Come for the hot chicken, stay for the heartburn.

Two blue-collar teams, two coaches who like it tough, and probably one last-minute kick.

My call: Browns 19, Titans 18.

MetLife Stadium, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS. The Dolphins are still looking for their first win and arrive rested off the bye. The Jets beat Cleveland two weeks ago, lost in Foxborough last Sunday, and would love a get-well game. Carla Ruiz talks Miami like a front-office insider who has seen two Lombardis and a few rebuilds. Mike Lasker speaks for the Jets, contrarian by birth, and he'll take any argument you've got.

Mike: Carla, welcome to New Jersey.

Carla: I thought we were playing the New York Jets.

Mike: We are. In New Jersey. Long story. We also share the building with the Giants, so if you see blue paint in the hallway, don't panic.

Carla: We'll manage. We flew in from a place where nobody owns a winter coat. And we still have the perfect season. You know the one. You have one Super Bowl, and it's a great one, I'll give you that.

Mike: Super Bowl III. The most famous upset ever, and a quarterback who guaranteed it out loud before kickoff. Contrarian to the core. You're 0-5. That's the only perfect thing about Miami this year.

Carla: Ouch. Fair, but ouch.

Last game, Dolphins: Before the bye, against Cincinnati, rookie receiver Kevin Coleman Jr. caught a fourth-quarter touchdown and made a 23-yard grab to set up another score. Miami's young secondary had a rough day against Joe Burrow, who completed passes to nine different receivers.

Carla: This is a teardown, and teardowns hurt. Jeff Hafley is building it with young players, and you can see pieces: Coleman, running back Ollie Gordon II. Willis said afterward the offense had to rethink what it does well, and the bye gave the staff two weeks to do it. I'm watching to see what they came up with.

Last week, Jets: New York lost 26-19 at New England, its fourth straight loss to the Patriots. David Bailey stripped TreVeyon Henderson to set up a field goal. But Smith threw his first interception of the season, the Jets went 0-for-3 in the red zone, and they were stopped on fourth-down runs on back-to-back possessions in the second quarter.

Mike: Aaron Glenn said afterward the Jets handed New England two touchdowns. I agree. But here's my contrarian take: that's the best the offense has looked in weeks. Cooper is a real weapon, Garrett Wilson is still Garrett Wilson, and Geno went 165 throws without an interception to start the year. Keep feeding Braelon Allen, who ran for 78 yards, and finish drives, and this team wins games.

The matchup: Miami's pass rush has been quiet. The Dolphins get to the quarterback on only 2.8% of dropbacks, and the Jets' blockers have allowed sacks on 9.7% of dropbacks. If Miami can't generate pressure, Smith will have all day to find Cooper and Wilson. On the other side, Miami runs for 5.0 yards a carry and the Jets allow 4.3, so expect plenty of Gordon. Bailey, Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick lead a Jets defense that would love to make Willis hold the ball.

The numbers: Miami has scored 70 points in five games and allowed 132. The Jets have scored 112 and allowed 122.

Mike: I'll be gracious. Come early, Carla. Our tailgates are legendary.

Carla: I'll bring sunscreen. Old habits.

Mike: You won't need it. It's New Jersey in late October.

Carla: Then I'll bring hope. It's the only thing a 0-5 team packs in every bag.

Two teams desperate for a turnaround, one division rivalry that goes back to the AFL, and a chance for somebody to feel good on Monday.

My call: Jets 24, Dolphins 16.

Sal: Mitch, I'll be honest. We have a pirate ship in our end zone with cannons on it, and lately they've been very quiet. That's on us.

Mitch: Quiet cannons. That's the saddest thing I've heard all week.

Sal: We also have two Super Bowl trophies and Lee Roy Selmon in the Hall of Fame. You have Julius Peppers and a lot of hope.

Mitch: Peppers is a first-ballot Hall of Famer and a North Carolina legend, so I'll take that trade. And our hope just won by 11 in Philadelphia.

Last week, Panthers: Carolina beat the Eagles 25-14. The Eagles were without Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley.

Egbuka against the Panthers' secondary is Tampa's best hope for big plays.

Sal: I regret everything I said in the first paragraph.

Two division rivals, a rookie trying to finish a game, and a Panthers team trying to prove last week wasn't a fluke.

My call: Panthers 28, Buccaneers 20.

Baltimore just lost a game it led 10-0 on a field goal with no time left, and now the Bengals walk in rested. Sounds like a spot to grab the points, right? Wrong. I'm laying them.

Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) at Baltimore Ravens (4-2), Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on CBS. The consensus has Baltimore −2.5 with a total of 51 (Oct 20, 12:52 UTC). My card: Baltimore Ravens −2.5, Under 51, and a final of Ravens 28, Bengals 21.

Why Baltimore? The Formula rates the Ravens at −0.3 and the Bengals at −6.2, then adds 1.75 for home field: Ravens by 7.6. That's three times the number you're laying. And look at how the Ravens lost in Cleveland: the defense did its job, and the game turned on one Derrick Henry fumble. Henry hadn't lost one all season. I'll take a team that loses like that.

Now, the elephant in the huddle. Lamar Jackson has missed two straight games with an ankle injury, and Tyler Huntley has started both, winning in overtime against Atlanta and losing by three in Cleveland. On Wednesday, Jackson was back at practice as a limited participant for the first time since he got hurt, and coach Jesse Minter said the work came with the full team. Minter still calls it day by day. One more name on the Ravens' report: outside linebacker Tavius Robinson, the team's sack leader, did not practice because of a pectoral injury. Lamar's status is still the one to watch, and if the news moves this number, you'll want to know before you do anything.

Why the Under? Cincinnati has allowed 109 points in five games. Baltimore's last game finished 13-10. The Formula's number is 47.7, and my final adds up to 49. Both are short of 51. The Bengals can light it up, sure. Joe Burrow spreads the ball around as well as anybody, and Ja'Marr Chase can win any one-on-one. But Cincinnati's run game averages 3.8 yards a carry, and Baltimore allows exactly 3.8. Burrow's going to have to grind for it.

Then the room started throwing elbows. Follow The Money makes no pick, but its market split is Ravens 27, Bengals 24, a three-point game. The Formula has Ravens 28, Bengals 20, an eight-point game.

Follow The Money went straight for the jugular: "Eight points? With Lamar day to day? You've got the Ravens winning a heavyweight fight with one glove."

The Formula shot right back: "And you've got a rested Bengals team hanging around all afternoon. Rest doesn't tackle anybody. Let's not throw a parade."

Next Man Up and Letdown Watch both sit at Ravens 28, Bengals 20 and are pretending not to hear any of this. In The Trenches passed on a pick, borrowed that same score and wisely stayed out of the crossfire.

games.fanatic_story:
AFC North Sunday at M&T Bank Stadium, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS. Cincinnati arrives rested off its bye. Baltimore arrives grumpy after a last-snap loss in Cleveland. Laura Kessel says every story starts with the quarterback. Owen Pratt says every story ends with the defense. Somebody is going to be wrong by Sunday night.

Owen: Welcome to Baltimore, Laura, the only city in the league that named its football team after a poem. Edgar Allan Poe lived here and is buried here. We have literature, we have crab cakes, and we have two Lombardi Trophies.

Laura: We have chili on spaghetti, and we're proud of it. And for the record, our franchise was founded by Paul Brown. We have socks older than your team.

Owen: Two Super Bowls, Laura. How many do you have?

Laura: We're pacing ourselves.

Last game, Bengals: Before the bye, Joe Burrow threw four touchdown passes in Miami, completing 23 of 32 to nine different receivers. Burrow also found tight ends Mike Gesicki and Tanner Hudson and running back Samaje Perine for scores. Safety Jordan Battle intercepted Malik Willis on back-to-back drives.

Laura: That's the whole philosophy. Give Joe time and he'll find somebody. Give him Ja'Marr and he'll find somebody spectacular.

Last week, Ravens: Baltimore led Cleveland 10-0 early and lost 13-10 on Andre Szmyt's 37-yard field goal on the final snap. Derrick Henry lost his first fumble of the season in the fourth quarter, and the Browns tied it on the next drive. Baltimore went scoreless on its final nine possessions.

Owen: It stung, and it stung more because Todd Monken, our offensive coordinator the last three years, was on the other sideline. But I'll tell you what I saw: our defense played well enough to win that game. Henry took the blame himself after the game. That's a pro. He'll be fine.

The big storyline: Lamar Jackson's ankle is still the status to watch, but Wednesday brought good news for Baltimore. He hurt it in the Week 4 win against Tennessee and has missed two games since. On Wednesday he was back at practice as a limited participant, his first work since the injury, and coach Jesse Minter said it was with the full team. Minter still calls it a day-by-day thing. The Ravens did lose a pass rusher for the day: outside linebacker Tavius Robinson, the team's sack leader, did not practice because of a pectoral injury. Huntley, who won a week earlier in overtime against Atlanta, is ready either way.

Laura: Quarterback-first, Owen. If Lamar plays, this is a heavyweight fight. If he doesn't, Joe Burrow is the best quarterback on the field, and it isn't close.

Owen: And Roquan Smith, Trey Hendrickson and Nnamdi Madubuike will be standing in his face asking him how close it is.

The matchup: Hendrickson against the Bengals offensive tackles is the headline, and yes, Bengals fans know exactly who Trey Hendrickson is. Chase against Marlon Humphrey and Nate Wiggins is the one you'll see on every highlight. On the other side, Cincinnati's front with Dexter Lawrence II and Jonathan Allen in the middle will try to do what Cleveland did: get Henry stopped early and make the Ravens throw.

The numbers: Baltimore has scored 156 and allowed 132 in six games. Cincinnati has scored 128 and allowed 109 in five.

Owen: Final word. The AFC North is a three-way tie at the top, and we're in it. Where are you?

Laura: Right behind you with a game in hand and a quarterback who just had a week off. Sleep well, Owen. Nevermore.

Owen: You can't quote Poe at me in my own building.

Laura: Watch me.

My call: Ravens 28, Bengals 21.

State Farm Stadium in Glendale, 4:05 p.m. Eastern on CBS. Denver arrives 4-2 with extra rest after a Thursday night win. Arizona arrives 2-4 and feeling great after stunning the Rams on the final play. Ruth Calder studies the Broncos through the life cycle of their quarterbacks. Neil Carver measures every Cardinals season against the year they reached the Super Bowl.

Neil: Ruth, welcome to the desert. Our roof retracts, and our grass field literally rolls outside to get some sun. Your field just sits there at altitude, gasping.

Ruth: Our field is a mile high, Neil. Visiting teams do the gasping. And we have three Super Bowl trophies to keep us company up there.

Neil: We have the oldest continuously run pro football franchise in America. We were wearing cardinal red before your grandparents were born.

Ruth: And you've been patiently waiting for a Super Bowl ever since.

Neil: We came close once. We'll talk about it again in February.

Last week, Broncos: Denver beat Seattle 17-14 in overtime on Thursday night. Ja'Quan McMillian intercepted Sam Darnold on Seattle's first overtime possession, and Wil Lutz kicked a 53-yard field goal to win it. Denver's defense hit Darnold 17 times, sacked him five times and intercepted him twice.

Ruth: Here's the honest life-cycle report. Nix is in his third season, and right now he's in the frustrating part, the one where defenses sit back and dare you to throw deep. He said as much after the game. Sean Payton said 4-2 could easily be 2-4. I appreciate a coach who can count. But Vance Joseph's defense is the real deal, and Pat Surtain II, Nik Bonitto and Zach Allen are why Denver keeps winning ugly.

Last week, Cardinals: Arizona went into SoFi Stadium having lost four straight and beat the Rams 18-16 on Chad Ryland's sixth field goal, a 43-yarder as time expired. It was first-year coach Mike LaFleur's first win against his old boss, Sean McVay, and Arizona's second win at SoFi this season.

Neil: Six field goals, Ruth. Six. It wasn't pretty, but a win in Los Angeles counts the same as a pretty one. This defense had given up a lot of points in the four games before that. It finally showed up.

The matchup: Neither team runs it well. Denver averages 3.6 yards a carry and Arizona 3.5, and both defenses allow more than that. Whoever gets the ground game going first may control this one. The Broncos' pass rush gets home on 7.9% of dropbacks, and Arizona's on 7.5%. Denver protects Nix well, allowing sacks on just 4.1% of dropbacks, so the Cardinals will have to win with coverage. McBride against Denver's linebackers is the matchup to watch. For Denver, Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton need to make the big plays Nix has been missing.

One more thing to know: Arizona hasn't won at home in more than a year, a run of losses that reached nine straight after a Week 5 loss to Detroit. Both of its wins this season came at SoFi Stadium.

The numbers: Denver has scored 114 and allowed 125. Arizona has scored 126 and allowed 178.

Ruth: So you're telling me you're better on the road in Los Angeles than at home?

Neil: We like the commute. Short flight, big wins.

Ruth: Bring a jacket if you ever visit Denver in October.

Neil: Bring sunscreen to Glendale. It's still summer here.

Two teams that win ugly, two kickers who just won games, and a Cardinals home crowd that would love to finally celebrate in its own building.

My call: Broncos 24, Cardinals 21.

Why the Chiefs? This is about as close as two teams get on paper. The Formula rates Kansas City at 4.1 and Seattle at 3. Give the Seahawks 1.75 for home field, one of the best in the league, and it's Seattle by 0.6. Less than a point. You're getting 2.5 with the better-rated team. I think Seattle wins a coin flip of a game, and I still want the points.

The matchup that seals it for me: Kansas City runs for 5.9 yards a carry. Seattle allows just 3.5, so something has to give, and the Chiefs have the guy who knows that defense best. Kenneth Walker III was Seattle's Super Bowl LX MVP in February, signed with Kansas City in March, and now leads the NFL in rushing. Meanwhile, Seattle's offense just got Sam Darnold hit 17 times in Denver, and Kansas City allows sacks on only 3.7% of dropbacks.

The caveats: Seattle had extra rest after playing Thursday, Lumen Field is a nightmare for visiting offenses, and Kansas City is banged up at receiver with Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton hurt. Sunday Night Football at Lumen Field, 8:20 p.m. Eastern on NBC. The unbeaten Chiefs visit the defending Super Bowl champions, and the man running the ball for Kansas City is the man who won Super Bowl LX's MVP award for Seattle eight months ago. Chet Morrell audits the Chiefs' dynasty like an accountant with a magnifying glass. Kara Holm speaks for the champs, and she's the first to tell you a ring doesn't play defense in October.

Kara: Chet, welcome to the loudest stadium in football. Bring earplugs. Our fans have set off seismic readings here, and I mean that literally.

Chet: We play at Arrowhead, Kara. We know loud. We also know trophies. We have a few lying around the house.

Kara: And we have the most recent one. Seahawks 29, Patriots 13, in February.

Chet: Which brings us to the awkward part. Kenneth Walker III. Your Super Bowl MVP. Our running back.

Kara: He signed with you in March, and I'll be honest, it still stings. But we'll cheer for him in warmups. Then we'd like him to have a very quiet evening.

Last week, Chiefs: Kansas City beat the Chargers 22-6 to stay unbeaten. Walker, who leads the NFL in rushing, ran for 128 yards and two touchdowns, including a 33-yard dash where he ran away from the last defender. Xavier Worthy caught seven passes for 73 yards, and Travis Kelce caught 53 yards' worth of passes despite briefly leaving with an ankle injury. Kansas City was missing receivers Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton, and right tackle Jaylon Moore left with a concussion. Andy Reid improved to 23-5 in regular-season games after a bye.

Chet: My audit says this: the defense held a team to six points, the run game finally has a bruiser, and Mahomes looks healthy. Harrison Butker missed an extra point and a field goal, which I've noted in red ink. A dynasty is a lot of little things done right.

Last week, Seahawks: Seattle lost 17-14 in overtime at Denver on Thursday night, its second loss in five days after a 32-29 home loss to San Francisco. The Broncos hit Sam Darnold 17 times and sacked him five times.

Kara: Mike Macdonald said his quarterback got hit way too much, and everybody could see it. He's right. Three losses already matches all of last season. I'm a champion's skeptic: rings are nice, but this team has to earn it again.

The matchup: This is a fascinating one. Kansas City runs for 5.9 yards a carry, and Seattle allows just 3.5. Walker against the defense he used to practice against every day is the headline. On the other side, Seattle's pass rush gets home on 8.2% of dropbacks, but the Chiefs allow sacks on only 3.7%. Leonard Williams, DeMarcus Lawrence and Byron Murphy II need to change that. Smith-Njigba against Chiefs corners Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane could be the matchup of the night. Seattle had extra rest after playing Thursday.

The numbers: Kansas City has scored 140 and allowed 83 in five games. Seattle has scored 148 and allowed 122 in six.

Chet: Last word, Kara. Seattle has a famous coffee culture. Kansas City has famous barbecue. Which one's better at 11 p.m. after a loss?

Kara: Coffee, because you're going to need to stay awake and think about what went wrong.

Chet: Ouch. Fine. Save me a cup.

The champs against the unbeatens, a reunion nobody in Seattle asked for, and a prime-time crowd ready to shake the ground.

My call: Seahawks 23, Chiefs 22.

The Cowboys just got shut out in the first half at Green Bay and threw two interceptions in scoring range.

The caveat: Philadelphia runs for just 3.8 yards a carry against a Dallas defense that allows 4.9, and In The Trenches takes Dallas because of it. Dallas also protects Dak Prescott well, allowing sacks on only 2.8% of dropbacks.

Why the Over? The Formula's number is 46.1, and my final adds up to 45. Dallas has scored 151 and allowed 159 in six games. That's a team whose games tend to have some points in them.

In The Trenches fired back: "Philly can't run, and Dallas doesn't give up sacks. That's the whole game. Points are a foreign language to you."

Then The Formula turned on Follow The Money: "And you, Cowboys by five, in Philadelphia, on Monday night? Bring a helmet."

Follow The Money's reply: "I'll bring two. One's for you." Next Man Up and Letdown Watch, parked right next to The Formula on the Eagles, pretended to check their phones.

Bottom of the card: two even teams, a road team laying more than it's earned, and a Monday night crowd that will be loud. Take the points and the Over.

games.fanatic_story:
Monday Night Football at Lincoln Financial Field, 8:15 p.m. Eastern on ESPN, ABC and Disney+. Cowboys and Eagles. Both 2-4. Both desperate. Neither town will admit the other one exists until kickoff. Cole Garrison speaks for Dallas and never confuses the brand with the results. Ray Donnelly speaks for Philadelphia and watches every snap of blocking twice.

Ray: Cole, I'll keep it simple. Super Bowl LIX. Eagles 40, Chiefs 22. What's the most recent one in Dallas?

Cole: It's been a while. I know. Five Super Bowls, Ray. Five. You have two.

Ray: And you've spent every year since your last one talking about logos and stadiums.

Cole: That's fair. The brand is enormous and the results have been, let's say, humble. I'm the guy who says it out loud. America's Team needs to start winning America's playoff games.

Ray: Meanwhile, our fans once booed Santa Claus, and we're proud of it.

Cole: That's not the flex you think it is.

Ray: It's exactly the flex I think it is. We're honest people, Cole. Loud, honest people.

Cole: Loud, I'll give you. I've sat in that building, and my ears are still ringing.

Last week, Cowboys: At Green Bay, CeeDee Lamb caught nine passes for 70 yards and George Pickens six for 73. The game had 22 penalties, 11 by each team. Brian Schottenheimer said afterward the Cowboys put themselves in a hole and have to work their way out.

Cole: The defense actually held up okay. The offense couldn't finish. Two interceptions in scoring range kills you against a good team, and that's on the quarterback and the coaches. Brand versus results, Ray. The results said 2-4.

Last week, Eagles: Jalen Hurts is on injured reserve with a blood clot in his calf and, according to the AP, will miss at least four games. Saquon Barkley missed his second straight game with a hamstring injury.

Ray: I watched the blocking twice, like always. It wasn't good. Miscommunication, wrong spots, a fumble that wasted a drive we needed. McKee said afterward he has to fix it, and I like that he owned it. But this is a team with Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Zack Baun and Quinyon Mitchell on defense. Get healthy and get organized, and this season is far from finished.

The big storyline: Quarterback availability. Hurts is on IR, Barkley's hamstring is the status to watch, and the first official injury report of the week isn't out yet.

The matchup: Philadelphia runs for just 3.8 yards a carry, while Dallas allows 4.9. If the Eagles can find a running game, McKee gets a lot more comfortable. Dallas protects Prescott well, allowing sacks on only 2.8% of dropbacks, so Vic Fangio's defense will have to win with coverage and disguise. Lamb against Mitchell is the marquee one-on-one. Dallas' defensive front, with Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark and Rashan Gary, gets a chance at an Eagles offense still finding its rhythm.

The numbers: Dallas has scored 151 and allowed 159. Philadelphia has scored 106 and allowed 137.

Cole: Last word, Ray. Philly cheesesteaks are great. I'll admit that on national television.

Ray: Texas brisket is great. I'll admit that too. Now please leave.

Cole: Love you too, Ray.

One of the fiercest grudges in the NFC East, two 2-4 teams, and a Monday night crowd in South Philly that will be heard from Broad Street to the Rio Grande.

My call: Cowboys 23, Eagles 22.
